takeaways: Biggest substantive issue: Paints/coatings. The architectural PRO/DIY split is very good, but automotive refinish appears under-allocated relative to the TAM scope.
Biggest channel issue: Pool chemicals/testing. Pool service/dealer/builder professionals should be a named core end market, not "Other," and a higher professional-share sensitivity is warranted.
Biggest taxonomy issue: Pest/turf/ag. Structural pest management should be its own professional route-service channel; pro turf/landscape/golf should be distinguished from specialty agriculture.
Strongest existing work: Floor & carpet care. The 80% facility/janitorial orientation is well supported; the next step is sub-segmentation, not a wholesale recut.

General cleaners are also directionally strong, but food & beverage processing sanitation deserves a distinct analytical lens because of compliance, dosing, CIP/open-plant cleaning and service intensity.
This is an outside-in audit of end-market allocation, not a replacement market model. Suggested ranges are intentionally broad where public data do not map cleanly to Claude's exact product scope.

I prioritized current industry associations, SEC filings/company presentations and recent market research. Manufacturer pages were used mainly to understand customer/application structure, not to size a market.

A recurring issue across categories is taxonomy: purchaser, applicator, channel and physical end-use are sometimes mixed. Before forcing percentages to 100%, Claude should choose one consistent dimension for the end-market table and use a separate channel table if needed.

Cross-category overlap should be explicitly flagged. Examples: floor disinfectants vs. the separate Disinfectants category; concrete sealers vs. coatings/waterproofing; automotive refinish inside special-purpose coatings; pool/water test kits crossing into water treatment and HVAC/R.
Where a range is shown, it is a sensitivity for Claude to test against SKU/channel evidence. It is not a directive to overwrite the existing number.

Scope consistency matters more than false precision. Several TAM anchors include factory/OEM or broad consumer demand, while the end-market table is organized around professional field users. That can mechanically distort pro share even if every individual percentage looks plausible.

'Facilities & Janitorial' is too broad in hygiene categories. Healthcare, education, foodservice, hospitality, BSC/commercial office and government have different chemistry, regulation, service models and willingness to pay.

'Other' should not hide strategic verticals. Controlled environments in wipes, OEM wood finishing in wood coatings, and food processing in disinfection are each large or economically distinctive enough to name.

Observed distributor SKU mix is useful evidence of channel presence, not revenue share. High-spec categories such as cleanroom wipes can generate many SKU variants and therefore look disproportionately large in a SKU-count view.
Wood finishes - Major challenge: Either add a 45-60% OEM/factory finishing lens or narrow the TAM. Current broad TAM + 15% OEM is internally inconsistent.
Hand cleaners / soaps / sanitizers - Challenge: 50% pro likely understates away-from-home institutional demand; add healthcare, foodservice and industrial/trades.
Disinfectants / sanitizers - Challenge taxonomy: Healthcare and food/contact sanitation should be explicit; professional share likely deserves 70-80% sensitivity for a pro-brand framing.
Roofing / waterproofing - Refine: Likely 85-90% pro/commercial; split new construction from reroof/restoration.
Wipes / wipers - Refine: Name controlled environments; revisit consumer share if mass consumer disinfecting wipes remain excluded.
Lubricants / oils - Mostly right: Keep overall mix but expose food processing and aviation/precision MRO.
Specialty janitorial - Mostly right: Keep ~90% pro but split the 78% Facilities bucket into real institutional verticals.

I would prioritize Claude's next edits as scope/taxonomy checks, not percentage replacement. Wood finishes is the clearest true mismatch. Hand hygiene and disinfectants need a more professional/institutional framing. Roofing likely needs a higher pro sensitivity. Wipes and lubricants mainly need better vertical labels. Specialty janitorial is directionally strong and mostly needs to be decomposed into actionable institutional end markets.
